sub: Germany's favourite shedding game: match the suit or the rank, use the 7, the 8 and the jack against the others – and don't forget to say “Mau”.
goal: The goal: be the first to get rid of all your cards. Say “Mau” before your last card – and “Mau-Mau” when you play it.

info.intro: Almost everyone in Germany, Austria and Switzerland grew up with Mau-Mau. If you know Uno or Crazy Eights, you already know half the rules – and the rest is explained in two minutes. One small pack of cards is all you need.

rules.setupLead: Mau-Mau is usually played with a 32-card Skat pack (7 to ace in four suits) and 2 to 6 players. Ranks don't beat each other – what counts is whether a card fits.
rules.dealP: Shuffle and deal 5 cards to everyone, one at a time. The rest go face down in the middle as the draw pile. Turn over the top card and put it next to it: that's the start of the discard pile.
rules.tableAlt: The draw pile face down, next to it the nine of spades face up as the first card.
rules.playLead: The player to the dealer's left starts, then it goes clockwise. On your turn you do exactly one thing:
rules.t1p: Put one card on the discard pile that matches the top card in suit (♠ on ♠) or in rank (9 on 9).
rules.t2p: If you can't play – or don't want to – draw one card from the draw pile. If it fits, you may play it straight away, otherwise your turn is over.
rules.t3p: Now it's the next player's turn. A special card can change that.
rules.ckQ: The 9 of spades is on top. What may you play?
rules.pileP: Take the discard pile, leave its top card where it is, shuffle the rest and put it face down as the new draw pile.
rules.spLead: Three ranks do something extra. They still have to fit by suit or rank – except the jack.
rules.sp7P: The next player has to draw 2 cards and can't play this turn. Unless they play a 7 themselves: then the following player draws 4, after a third 7 it's 6, and so on.
rules.sp8P: The next player is skipped and it's the turn of the player after them. With two players, you simply play again.
rules.spjP: A jack fits on any card. Whoever plays it names a suit, and the next player has to follow that suit (or play another jack, if your group allows it).
rules.spNote: A jack can't be played on a 7 that still has to be paid: first draw the cards, then the game goes on normally.
rules.mauLead: The cards are only half the game – you also have to talk.
rules.mauAlt: With one card left in your hand you say Mau, with your last card you say Mau-Mau.
rules.mauWhen1: when you play your second-to-last card
rules.mauWhen2: when you play your last card
rules.mauP: Forgot to say it? If someone notices before the next player has played, you draw a penalty card – in many groups two. That also applies to your very last card: you draw instead of winning, and the game goes on.
rules.scLead: Whoever has played their last card wins the round. If you play several rounds, the others count the cards still in their hand:
rules.scP: Write down the points after each round. Whoever reaches an agreed limit first – 100 points, say – loses the game, and the player with the fewest points wins. Simpler: count only the rounds won.
rules.varLead: Mau-Mau has endless house rules – from region to region and from table to table. Agree on them before the first card. The most common ones:
rules.var1: Ace instead of 8: in many places the ace is the skip card and the 8 is a normal card.
rules.var2: 9 turns: a 9 reverses the direction of play.
rules.var3: Jack on jack: forbidden in many groups (known in Germany as “Bube auf Bube stinkt”), allowed in others.
rules.var4: No jack at the end: you may not go out with a jack. Whoever tries draws a penalty card.
rules.var5: Ace again: after an ace the same player plays once more.
rules.var6: Draw until it fits: instead of one card you keep drawing until you can play.
rules.var7: 10 with a twist: after a 10 the next player has to play the same suit or a 10 – no jack.
rules.var8: 6 cards: deal 6 cards each instead of 5 for a longer round.
rules.var9: Pass on the 7s: whoever has to draw for a 7 may also counter with an 8 (usually of the same suit) and pass the cards on to the next player.
rules.faq1q: May I draw even though I could play?
rules.faq1a: Yes, in most groups you may. Sometimes it's clever to keep a jack or a 7 for later.
rules.faq2q: What happens if the first card turned over is a special card?
rules.faq2a: Usually it counts for the first player: a 7 makes them draw 2, an 8 skips them, a jack lets them play any suit. Some groups just turn over another card.
rules.faq3a: Yes, that's the standard rule: each further 7 adds 2 cards for the next player. Only whoever can't or won't play a 7 has to draw them all – see Special cards.
rules.faq4q: Does the suit I wish for with a jack have to be in my hand?
rules.faq4a: No, you can wish for any suit. It's usually smart to choose the suit you have most of.
rules.faq5q: How is Mau-Mau different from Uno?
rules.faq5a: Uno is the commercial cousin with its own pack and colours. The idea is the same: match by colour or number, special cards for draw, skip and wish. Mau-Mau only needs an ordinary pack of cards.
rules.faq6q: What else is the game called?
rules.faq6a: In Switzerland Tschau Sepp, in English-speaking countries Crazy Eights (with the 8 as the wish card), in the Netherlands Pesten.
rules.faq7q: Can I play Mau-Mau with 52 cards?
rules.faq7a: Yes. The rules stay the same, the cards from 2 to 6 simply have no special effect and count their face value when scoring. With 52 cards up to 8 players can join in.

strategy.sub: Anyone can drop the first card that fits. Keeping suit options open, holding your 7 and jack for the right moment and reading what the others draw wins far more rounds.
strategy.principle: Good Mau-Mau is about flexibility and timing. Every ordinary card you play should either shed high penalty points, keep your suits balanced or steer the table away from the next player’s strength.
principleItems: Keep suit variety early. Holding three or four different suits means you rarely have to draw.
Save special cards for moments that hurt. A 7 or jack spent on turn one won’t be there when someone calls “Mau!” or sends a +2 chain your way.
Shed heavy points when you have a choice. Aces (11) and 10s (10) cost a lot if another player goes out before you.
strategy.handLead: Whenever more than one card fits the discard pile, the order you play them in shapes the next three turns.
strategy.exH: Example: four cards fit – which one goes first?
strategy.exAlt: The 9 of spades lies on the pile. Your hand holds the ace of spades (outlined as best play), queen of spades, 9 of hearts and jack of clubs.
strategy.exWhy: Play the ace of spades (A♠). It clears 11 penalty points right away, keeps the queen of spades in hand so you can still follow spades, keeps the 9 of hearts to switch suits later and saves your jack for an emergency.
handItems: Dump high points inside the same suit. Holding ♠A (11) and ♠Q (3)? Play the ace first – both match spades, and if someone goes out next turn you lose 3 points instead of 11.
Play out of your longest suit first. If you hold three clubs and one diamond, stay in clubs while you can – once your single diamond is gone, you can no longer follow diamonds.
Keep rank bridges. A card whose rank matches another suit in your hand (like ♥9 and ♠9) lets you change suits cleanly without spending a jack.
Drawing voluntarily can pay off. If your only playable card is a jack or your last 7 early in a large round, taking one card from the draw pile is sometimes smarter than burning your defense.
strategy.spLead: Only three ranks carry special effects in Mau-Mau – treat them like tools, not ordinary cards.
strategy.sp7p: Keep one 7 in reserve as insurance against a 7-chain: stacking your 7 passes +4 cards on instead of ruining your own hand. Attack with a 7 when the next player has only one or two cards left – especially right after they call “Mau!”.
strategy.sp8h: 8 – Stop the leader (or chain in a duel)
strategy.sp8p: Save an 8 to skip a neighbour who is about to win, giving the rest of the table another chance to change the suit or drop a 7. In a two-player game an 8 gives you an immediate extra turn – pair it with a matching final card to close the round on the spot.
strategy.spJh: Jack – Emergency exit and endgame closer
strategy.spJp: A jack fits any card (except an open 7), yet costs 20 penalty points if caught in your hand. Hold it to rescue dead suits or steer into your last card’s suit – and if you play for points and someone calls “Mau!”, dump the jack before the round ends.
strategy.wishLead: Playing a jack is only half the move – the suit you name can lock down the whole table.
wishItems: Wish for your strongest suit. Early and mid-round, name the suit you hold most of so you can keep playing without drawing.
Watch what opponents draw on. If the next player just had to draw on diamonds, wish diamonds – you force them to draw again and buy yourself tempo.
Set up your final card. Down to two cards including a jack? Play the jack now and wish the exact suit of your last card (don’t forget to say “Mau!”).
strategy.wishWarn: Check house rules before holding a jack for last: many groups forbid going out on a jack (“No jack at the end”) or stacking “jack on jack”. In those rounds, always play your jack second-to-last, never as your final card.
strategy.endLead: The last two cards – and the two magic words – decide close rounds.
endItems: Build a clean two-card finish. Aim to keep two cards that share a suit, share a rank, or pair an 8 or jack with your closer.
Slow down for “Mau!” and “Mau-Mau!”. More rounds are lost to a forgotten call than to bad luck. Say “Mau!” as you lay down your second-to-last card and “Mau-Mau!” on your last.
Switch to damage control when playing for points. The second another player calls “Mau!” and you can’t stop them with a 7 or 8, drop your jack (20), ace (11) or 10 (10) immediately.
mistakes: Burning a jack on turn one. Playing a jack when a normal card fits throws away your best escape hatch for nothing.
Dropping your only 7 with no threat. Sending out a lone 7 early leaves you defenseless when a +2 chain comes back around the table.
Playing a queen instead of an ace of the same suit. Keeping an 11-point ace while shedding a 3-point queen hurts badly if someone goes out suddenly.
Ignoring what suits opponents drew on. Every draw tells you a suit that player is missing – use that information when you play a jack.
Forgetting to say “Mau!” or “Mau-Mau!”. One penalty card on your winning play can hand the whole round to the next player.
Holding a jack as your last card under strict house rules. If “No jack at the end” is active, finishing on a jack costs you a penalty card instead of winning.

quick.rule: 5 cards each (32-card pack). Play 1 card matching the top card’s suit or rank – or draw 1 (play right away if it fits). First empty hand wins.
quick.sp8: Skip the next player (2 players: go again)
quick.spJ: Make a wish: fits any card (not an open 7) – choose the next suit
quick.mau1: “Mau!” – say it on your second-to-last card (forgot = penalty card)
quick.mau2: “Mau-Mau!” – say it on your last card to win the round
